candidate.educational_objective: Explain the cancer-prevention purpose and current routine schedule of HPV vaccination for an immunocompetent preteen, including why vaccination is given before likely HPV exposure and why it applies regardless of sex.

options.A: HPV vaccination is routinely recommended at age 11–12 years because it prevents new HPV infections that can cause cancers later in life; when started at ages 9–14, the routine series is 2 doses 6–12 months apart.
options.B: HPV vaccination should be delayed until adulthood because it works best only after a person has already been exposed to HPV.
options.C: HPV vaccine is used to treat an existing HPV infection, so it is started only after an HPV-related lesion or abnormal screening result develops.
options.D: HPV vaccination is recommended only for girls because HPV-related cancers do not occur in boys or men.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. The current CDC child/adolescent immunization schedule notes routine HPV vaccination at age 11–12 years, with vaccination permitted starting at age 9. For people who initiate vaccination at ages 9–14 years, the routine schedule is 2 doses at 0 and 6–12 months; immunocompromised persons require a 3-dose series. CDC also states that HPV vaccination prevents new HPV infections rather than treating existing infection or disease and protects against HPV infections that cause cancers in both females and males. B is incorrect because vaccination is most beneficial before exposure. C reverses prevention and treatment. D is incorrect because HPV causes cancers in both men and women and vaccination is recommended for all preteens.
candidate.source_claim_supported: CDC currently supports routine HPV vaccination at ages 11–12, a 2-dose 0 and 6–12 month series when initiated at ages 9–14 for immunocompetent persons, prevention of new HPV infection rather than treatment, and cancer-prevention benefit for both males and females.
